title: Managing potential environmental and human health risks of lead halide perovskite photovoltaic modules
abstract: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) are emerging photovoltaic (PV) technologies capable of matching power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) of current PV technologies in the market at lower manufacturing costs, making perovskite solar modules (PSMs) cost competitive if manufactured at scale and perform with minimal degradation. PSCs with the highest PCEs, to date, are lead halide perovskites. Lead presents potential environmental and human health risks if PSMs are to be commercialized, as the lead in PSMs are more soluble in water compared to other PV technologies. Therefore, prior to commercialization of PSMs, it is important to highlight, identify, and establish the potential environmental and human health risks of PSMs as well as develop methods for assessing the potential risks. Here, we identify and discuss a variety of international standards, U.S. regulations, and permits applicable to PSM deployment that relate to the potential environmental and human health risks associated with PSMs. The potential risks for lead and other hazardous material exposures to humans and the environment are outlined which include water quality, air quality, human health, wildlife, land use, and soil contamination, followed by examples of how developers of other PV technologies have navigated human health and environmental risks previously. Potential experimentation, methodology, and research efforts are proposed to elucidate and characterize potential lead leaching risks and concerns pertaining to fires, in-field module damage, and sampling and leach testing of PSMs at end of life. Lastly, lower technology readiness level solutions to mitigate lead leaching, currently being explored for PSMs, are discussed. PSMs have the potential to become a cost competitive PV technology for the solar industry and taking steps toward understanding, identifying, and creating solutions to mitigate potential environmental and human health risks will aid in improving their commercial viability.

## **1. Introduction**

Over the past decade, metal halide perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as one of the next potential advancements in solar energy technology. PSCs offer the ability to be manufactured at low costs with techniques like physical or chemical vapor deposition or solution processes that are compatible with roll-to-roll manufacturing techniques. The challenge is to scale-up PSCs and perovskite solar modules (PSMs) while maintaining a power conversion efficiency (PCE) comparable to other photovoltaic (PV) modules on the market [1,2]. The best PCE for a PSC confirmed by an independent, recognized testing lab in 2013 was ~14 % (Ecole Polytechnique F[ ́]  ́ed ́erale de Lausanne) and increased to 26.1 % (University of Science and Technology of China) in 2023 [3]. The PCE for PSCs has been demonstrated to increase further to 33.7 % when

paired with crystalline silicon (c-Si) in a tandem cell configuration [3]. Furthermore, the estimated cost of manufacturing PSCs are $31.7/ m[2] –$38.7/m[2 ] compared to $62.9/m[2] –$79.3/m[2 ] for c-Si, making PSCs a potentially cost effective technology for solar power generation [4,5].

While the demonstrated PCEs and projected manufacturing costs make integrating PSCs into the solar energy market attractive, very few or no PSCs have been packaged into full-size PV modules and commercialized to date. Market penetration has been difficult due to device instability and short service life expectancies compared to market ready c-Si or cadmium-telluride (CdTe) PV modules [6]. However, the solar energy community is already searching for solutions to many of the issues that cause device instability and short service life expectancies, such as improved deposition methods to reduce defects [7–9], improved encapsulants and edge seals to mitigate water absorption, improved

Once these challenges are overcome, PSMs will need to meet several general PV product and quality standards and bankability requirements that pertain to manufacturing quality, construction, and reliability, specifically International Organization for Standards (ISO) 9001, International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) 61730-1, IEC 61730-2, and IEC 62941 to name a few [14–16]. Since PSMs are in their nascency, commercial standards specific to PSMs are not yet in place, but many researchers working towards commercialization are utilizing protocols set by the International Summit on Organic Photovoltaic Stability to evaluate performance [17]. It is expected that as the technology moves towards commercialization, new standards may emerge that include light and elevated temperature testing which are not present in IEC standards for existing PV technology.

As the manufacturing, module stability, and bankability barriers are being addressed, PSM manufacturers will additionally need to address the unique potential environmental and human health risks of PSMs to allay concerns of lead toxicity and/or other hazardous materials during manufacturing, service life, and end of life (EoL) management. The highest performing and most commercially viable PSMs contain lead as a constituent in the crystallographic structure. This poses potential environmental and human health risks, as lead ions present in PSMs are more soluble in water and are more readily absorbed into biological systems than other PV technologies [18–20]. Other toxic constituents that could be present in PSMs are tin, chromium, and cesium, and some PSM manufacturing processes use toxic solvents such as N,Ndimethylformamide (DMF), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and N- methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) that also pose potential environmental and human health risks [18,21,22].

Lead is a leading concern due to its higher solubility than other PV technologies that could lead to potential environmental and human health risks throughout the PSM value chain. A typical lead-containing PSM could contain ~0.4–2 g/m[2 ] [23,24]. For a 5 MW utility scale solar farm with 45,000 m[2 ] of PSM surface area, the entire farm would contain 18–90 kg of lead contained within the modules [25]. It should be noted that other highly utilized products in use today contain lead such as 6.1 million lead pipe service lines for potable water systems in the U. S. and lead acid batteries [26]. For example, lead found in a lead acid battery of an automobile is roughly ~54 % – ~ 70 % of the total battery mass [27]. Assuming an average lead acid battery has a mass of 17.7 kg, – a single automobile battery contains ~9.5 kg 12.4 kg of lead which would be between 10 % and 69 % of the mass of lead that could be found in the entire 5 MW perovskite solar farm example mentioned above [28].

Other PV technologies such as c-Si PV modules contain lead primarily in metallization pastes as well as the solders that attach the tabs to the fingers and busbars [29]. Compared to PSMs, c-Si modules have – comparable, if not greater, masses of lead per area (~2 8 g/m[2] ), just in a less mobile/soluble form [30,31]. Other thin-film PV modules (e.g., CdTe and copper indium gallium diselenide) do not contain much lead, if any, although many do contain other toxic metals like cadmium, gallium, tellurium, selenide, etc. [24,29,30,32].

The higher water solubility of lead in PSMs poses a unique set of potential environmental and human health risks that are not posed by existing thin-film and c-Si modules [18,33]. Beyond potential exposure to workers directly handling the modules during manufacturing, installation, and EoL management, lead in PSMs has the potential to leach out into the environment through rainfall if the integrity of the module assembly is compromised (i.e., broken). If PSMs are damaged in the field from installation, transportation, or extreme weather the possibility of lead leaching increases with subsequent rainfall or flooding as water will have ingress pathways [18,34]. Lead that leaches out of the module poses a potential contamination risk to the soil and groundwater where it could be further transferred to plants, wildlife, or humans depending on the site. Strategies, such as encapsulants, can be employed in the module design to mitigate lead leaching in PSMs but damage from

extreme weather and transportation or manufacturing defects could still allow for water ingress.

The main objective of this article is to identify and discuss possible solutions for managing potential environmental and human health risks of PSMs. An overview of PSMs and potential environmental and human health risks will be summarized to identify the specific potential risks and concerns followed by a review of international PV product standards and U.S environmental and human health safety regulations that apply to PSMs during manufacturing, transportation, installation, operation, decommissioning, and EoL management. Following the regulation, standards, and permit review, examples of how other commercialized PV technologies overcame environmental and human health risks are discussed. Next, suggestions for physical tests and future work that could be conducted to provide an understanding and basis for assessing the potential environmental and human health risks of PSMs during the commercialization process are discussed. Lastly, potential solutions that address and mitigate the risks are highlighted.

## **2. Overview of perovskite solar cell technology and potential environmental and human health risks**

A perovskite is a material identified by its crystal structure with the general formula of ABX3 with “A” on the vertices, “B” in the center, and “X” on the faces of a cubic unit cell [35]. By definition, many materials are considered perovskites regardless of whether they are PV materials or not, such as CaTiO3. For a PSC absorber layer material, the “A” is typically an organic cation or cesium, the “B” is a cation with a smaller atomic radius than “A”, and the “X” is a halogen which is commonly iodine, bromine, or chlorine. In halide perovskites, which are most of the studied PSCs, the “A” units are commonly CH3NH+3 , CH5N+2 or Cs+, the “B” units are commonly Pb[2][+] or Sn[2][+] , and the “X” units are commonly I[−] , Br[−] , Cl[−] [35] A PSC device is comprised of metal electrodes, a hole transport layer (HTL), a perovskite semiconductor, an electron transport layer (ETL), and a substrate. The PSCs can be formed into modules via scribing of individual PV cells and sandwiched between two glass covers, encapsulant layers, and a polyisobutene (PIB) edge sealant around the glass perimeter [18]. The encapsulant layer inside the glass can potentially include a sequestration layer to mitigate lead or other hazardous material from leaching. While several other metals can be substituted for lead like tin, cesium, and chromium, these substitutes do not offer comparable PCEs, increasing the levelized cost of energy and decreasing the cost competitiveness of perovskite PV technology in the market [1,3,5,6,9].

PSCs can be manufactured utilizing a variety of vapor deposition or solution-based techniques. Since the solution-based techniques are more compatible with roll-to-roll processing, solution processing is the most widely utilized set of techniques which involves a series of solvent depositions followed by heating to create perovskite layers on a substrate [2]. Solvent selection plays an important role in manufacturability and overall quality of the PSC, but can also be a potential human health risk if safety controls and measures are not established. DMF, DMSO, and NMP are all solvents that have been previously used for PSC manufacturing that are easily absorbed through the skin and can be carcinogenic and reprotoxic, but may be able to be replaced with safer options upon further research [18,21,22,36].

One of the first metal halide PSCs using a methylammonium lead iodide (MAPI) formulation was developed by Kojima _et al._ in 2009, reporting a PCE of 3.8 % [37]. In recent years, the more common metal halides are formamidinium lead iodide (FAPI) with simulations showing PCEs up to 26.48 % depending on the ETL and HTL selections [38]. Even with the PCE improvements, both MAPI and FAPI-containing PSCs degrade in the presence of light, heat, and water, commonly resulting in lead-based by-products such as lead iodide, lead hydroxide, lead phosphate, and lead carbonate [39–44].

## **3. Application of current product standards and environment and safety regulations to PSMs**

There are currently no environmental, health and safety standards and regulations pertaining specifically to PSMs, but many standards and regulations exist that would apply to the potential environmental and human health risks of PSMs. Table 2 outlines the main standards and regulations regarding the environmental and human health risks that would apply to PSMs in the U.S, if commercially available and deployed today. Each step in the PSM value chain has specific potential environmental and human health risks that would be regulated and standardized by many governing organizations such as, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), United States Department of Energy (USDOE), Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), IEC, ISO, United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), and state and local governments. Since lead leaching is one of the leading potential environmental and human health risks associated with PSMs, many of the water and air quality, human and wildlife health, and waste management regulations, mentioned in Table 2, pertain to lead exposure regulations which are defined in Table 3 along with other relevant exposure limits and criteria.

## _3.1. Water quality_

Many of the water quality regulations that would apply to the potential environmental and human health risks associated with PSMs are administered by the EPA through the Clean Water Act (CWA) that regulates the discharge of pollutants to U.S. waters, Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) that regulates pollutant concentrations in drinking water, and the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) that regulates the amount and type of effluent allowed to be discharged [45,46,57]. The applicability to PSMs has relevance at the manufacturing stage where toxic solvents utilized during manufacturing have the potential to be discharged or find pathways to ground water sources. In the operational and EoL stages, broken or damaged modules may have the potential to leach lead into the surrounding groundwater which would need to not surpass the thresholds in Table 3.

## _3.3. Human health_

OSHA who regulates work safety and IEC and ISO who creates standards for manufacturing and performance quality that apply to current and future PV technologies have regulations and standards in place that would pertain to PSMs to help mitigate potential environmental and human health risks. The specific OSHA standards related to PSMs are 1910.1025 and 1926.62 that regulate lead exposure levels per volume over an 8-hour workday that may apply to any handling or exposure from a mechanical operation being performed to a PSM [49,50]. While the IEC and ISO standards apply to the manufacturing stage of the value chain, the OSHA regulations should be considered throughout the entire value chain of PSMs.

## _3.4. Waste_

Regulations for solid waste from EoL management of PSMs or scrap disposal from manufacturing processes are administered by the EPA through the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA). The RCRA regulates hazardous waste, specifies methods for characterizing hazardous wastes, and mandates how hazardous waste is handled and disposed [52]. According to RCRA 261.24, wastes including PV modules or solar panels (which would include PSMs) are characterized as hazardous waste if the results of EPA’s Toxicity Characteristic Leaching Procedure (TCLP) Test Method 1311, a chemical analysis of organic and inorganic contaminants, are greater than or equal to any of the RCRA defined toxic material concentrations [52,59]. For lead, the threshold value is 5 mg/L (Table 3). To standardize and reduce the variability in TCLP testing, the American Society for Testing Materials (ASTM)

Standard E3325-21 was developed to define where and how to extract samples of existing PV module technology for TCLP testing [60]. Since ASTM E3325-21 calls for waterjet cutting of PV modules, it is uncertain how the standard will translate to PSMs as PSM lead solubility is greater than c-Si module lead solubility in water. More discussion on this topic can be found in section 5.3. If a PSM is determined to be hazardous waste, additional cost, permitting, storage, and specialty transportation will be required to remove the PSMs from the solar site [52,61].

## _3.5. Wildlife considerations and land use_

An incidental take permit will need to be issued by the USFWS, if potential risks of lead leaching to the soil and/or groundwater from PSMs could harm or harass a threatened and endangered species by causing habitat modification or degradation that significantly impairs essential behaviors [54]. There are no set contamination limits, to our knowledge, in which certain lead levels would be acceptable and would likely be subject to determination by the USFWS on a case-by-case basis. For land use, soil contamination regulation is administered by the EPA through the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) that would apply to PSMs if lead leaching is a possibility in the installation, operation, and EoL management stages of the value chain [62]. The other land use consideration is the state and local permitting that would be necessary for developing a PSM farm. The processes and mechanisms that are required for granting local and state permits/ordinances for developing a PSM farm would be different depending on the state, county, municipality, and local public perception of solar energy and PSMs specifically [55,56].

## **4. Takeaways from other commercialized PV module types**

To better understand how to commercialize and navigate the associated and potential environmental and human health risks of new PV technologies, lessons from previously commercialized PV technologies can be leveraged. One of the more recent developments of PV technologies are CdTe PV modules, commercialized by First Solar, Inc. Cadmium is defined as a toxic, carcinogenic, and hazardous material by the U.S. EPA and U.S. Center for Disease Control and Prevention [18,29,63,64]. While tellurium isn’t considered to be a toxic or hazardous material by the EPA, it has still been linked with several human health issues such as kidney, heart, lung, and gastrointestinal damage [64].

To help mitigate the risk of cadmium leaching and exposure to humans and the environment, First Solar, Inc. developed a recycling process specific to their CdTe PV modules and takeback service for EoL modules. Facilitating a recycling pathway for customers provides an option for CdTe PV modules to avoid the landfill, potential environmental contamination, and provides an opportunity for the CdTe PV module materials to be incorporated back into their respective material streams. First Solar, Inc.’s recycling process involves mechanical recycling followed by separation techniques to remove the thin film metals (Cd and Te) from the glass and backsheet. Over 90 % of the glass and over 90 % of the thin film semiconductor material can be recovered [65]. Providing an easily accessible recycling service in addition to the sale of thin film PV modules allows for certainty in EoL management, ease of handling if deemed as hazardous waste, and increased circularity within the solar industry.

Another strategy that can be taken from CdTe PV modules and translated to PSMs to help mitigate potential environmental and human health risks is reducing the risk of module breakage during shipping and installation [18,66,67]. A damaged module, whether it is detected or not, poses unanticipated potential risks to human health and environmental safety through potential leaching of hazardous materials. Methods to combat damage during transportation or installation could be accomplished through the development of packaging specifically designed for the PV module and the development of a robust standard

operating procedure for installing PV modules that focuses on minimizing damage [10,18,68–70].

Beyond CdTe PV modules, the development and maturing of the recycling infrastructure for solar power will help aid in keeping all types of PV modules out of landfills, decreasing the potential risk of hazardous materials leaching into soil and groundwater [71,72]. As of 2023, the U. S. has approximately 40 PV module recyclers, though some only recover the frame, junction box, and cabling and do not recycle the module laminate. A review of PV recycling patents suggests that ~80 % target c- Si modules, ~6 % target CdTe modules, and ~5 % target Copper Indium Gallium Diselenide (CIGS) modules [73]. Perovskites and other emerging PV technologies are not well-represented in patents yet, but recent research suggests PSM recycling would be cost-effective and enable material recovery for reuse in new PSM products [74]. Additionally, several researcher groups view mandatory PSM recycling as essential to future commercialization of perovskite PV technology [75–79]. Based on the progression of PV module recycling and PSM commercialization, it is likely that recycling technology specifically for PSMs will develop and become available to handle EoL PSMs. Many strategies and experiences from the current PV module fleet can be leveraged to help mitigate the potential environmental and human health risks associated with PSMs and help expedite the bankability and commercialization of the technology.

## **5. Potential environment and human health risk assessments**

While there may be potential environmental and human health risks for PSC and PSM manufacturing processes, the experimentation and methodologies mentioned here are focused on assessing the potential environmental and human health risks of operating PSM farms and managing PSMs at EoL. The testing and methodologies described in this review are meant to be utilized as a guide and starting points for experimental design. The testing to be considered here to evaluate the potential environmental and human health risks includes smoke toxicity and burned module leach testing, in-field PSM module damage simulation coupled with leach testing, custom sampling techniques for leach testing of PSMs, and correlating PSM damage to likelihood of lead or other hazardous material leaching. Many of these exposure pathways are highly influenced by module construction and design, which have not yet been established for PSMs, but may be subject to change as the technology readiness level (TRL) increases. Once higher TRL PSMs emerge, such testing would be warranted.

## _5.1. Fire testing_

Solar PV modules encounter potential fire risks from a variety of sources such as wildfires, house fires for rooftop modules, weather events, etc. To understand the potential risks of fire on human and environmental health, burn testing can be employed to simulate fire damage to PSMs. Air emissions and leachate from fire-damaged modules can be assessed to determine the potential human and environmental risks from the smoke and lead leaching after extinguishing (Fig. 2). The smoke will consist of a gaseous phase that contains mostly organic compounds and PM phase that contains mostly inorganic compounds. During the burn testing, flammability characteristics can be measured, and smoke samples can be collected. Furthermore, the collected data from the burn testing can be utilized as inputs for Gaussian plume dispersion modeling or other dispersion modeling to understand the toxicity hazards of the smoke plume with respect to distance from the smoke source (Fig. 2a) [31].

A calorimeter can be employed to initiate the burn testing and collect information on temperature, mass loss rates, and heat transfer. Once smoke production occurs, smoke production rate can be characterized and smoke samples can be collected to characterize the gaseous and PM compositions, concentrations, and particle size distribution (PM only). To characterize the PM phase of the smoke, inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy and inductively coupled plasma mass spectroscopy are possible techniques to employ to determine concentrations of inorganic elements such as lead [80]. The particle number and size distribution are also able to be characterized via an engine exhaust particle sizer or a cascade impactor [81,82]. Depending on how the sampling is performed, concentrations for TEELs can be calculated which would help provide necessary insight to emergency responders and owners (terrestrial or rooftop) about toxicity hazards caused from the smoke in case of a fire. All the collected data may be utilized in a computational model such as a Gaussian plume model or the EPA developed AEROMOD smoke dispersion model to estimate the contamination risk of smoke generated from a PSM fire downwind [31,83].

Another factor to be considered once a fire has occurred is the possibility for lead to leach out while extinguishing the fire or in the event of rainfall after a fire has occurred. Once fire testing is completed, burned modules can be sampled for TCLP testing and compared to pristine modules to help determine if burned modules exposed to water are more or less likely to be classified as hazardous waste. A synthetic precipitation leaching procedure (SPLP) test or water leach test (WLT), which is designed to evaluate the contamination impact of hazardous materials on soil or groundwater due to standard rainfall, can be conducted on the collected extinguishing water to determine concentrations of lead to help assess the potential risk of groundwater contamination (Fig. 2b) [84,85]. Table 4 summarizes the equipment and characterization options and opportunities for assessing the environmental and human health risks of fire-related events for PSMs.

The tests and techniques to characterize potential risks discussed here can be employed at a variety of scales depending on the TRL of the PSM. Testing of perovskite devices at the cell or coupon level can

provide initial insights on fire, runoff water, and material leaching characteristics, but lab scale specimens may not be representative of commercial module assemblies. The fire and leach testing at multiple scales may be valuable in understanding potential environmental and human health risks during product development allowing for design changes to help mitigate concerns as the technology and product development progresses.

## _5.2. In-field damage simulation_

Encapsulations and sequestration layers are applicable technologies to mitigate potential lead leaching from PSMs [18]. However, if the encapsulations and sequestration layers become damaged postproduction or have defects, then the potential for lead leaching to the soil or groundwater increases through the creation of water ingress pathways. Potential scenarios that could cause PSM breakage include transportation damage, damage during installation (such as over torquing when mounting) or maintenance activities, wind loading, or extreme weather events [18,91,92]. Water from rainfall may also be able to access the lead-containing layers of the perovskite device due to faulty module design or poor manufacturing quality. Any of these may result in moisture ingress and subsequent potential lead leaching to the soil or groundwater. The degree of leaching and potential for environmental and human health risks depend on the extent of module damage, environmental exposure (e.g., amount of rainfall), site location, soil characteristics, and other factors [23,93].

Even though damage can come from a variety of sources, many if not all can be simulated and tested to help understand the potential risk of lead leaching. We chose to highlight two potential experimental test designs with subsequent analyses here: 1) simulated rainfall testing of aged PSMs and 2) hail strike testing of PSMs. Rainfall simulation and subsequent SPLP testing or WLT of the rainwater once it runs off the PSM taken at intermittent rainfall amounts could build an understanding of the extent of possible lead leaching from PSMs during rainfall. To further understand how the extent of possible lead leaching may change over time during service, the rainfall simulation testing could be performed on several PSMs that have undergone different amounts of accelerated aging making the test more representative of modules in the field

## _5.3. Sampling and leach testing_

The classification of PV modules as hazardous waste depends on whether the concentrations of the defined substances measured with EPA recognized methods (e.g. TCLP testing) exceed the RCRA limits. The method for sampling PV modules can have a major effect on the results of the TCLP test as only a 100 g sample of the overall PV module is sent for TCLP testing. Following ASTM E3325-21 helps improve precision and repeatability of results through proportional sampling of the module using waterjet cutting. However, for PSMs, the lead halide structure is more water soluble than other PV technologies, potentially risking lead contamination to the water used for waterjet cutting and inaccurate TCLP analyses.

One research need is to identify alternative TCLP sample extraction equipment and methodologies that do not utilize water, such as a circular saw, creating surface scratches to guide fracturing, or use of other cutting tools. With further research into alternative sample extraction methods, ASTM 3325-21 could be modified to include a non-water jet cutting standard operating procedure for PSMs. Beyond sampling pristine PSMs for TCLP testing, aged modules could also be sampled to understand how aging might affect variability in TCLP testing. Accelerated aging or damage simulation could be employed to explore how degradation, such as delamination, microcracks, etc. allows moisture ingress and creates more pathways for leaching (Fig. 5). ## **6. Potential solutions for risk mitigation**

To enhance the commercialization potential of PSMs, several strategies are being researched to improve module stability and mitigate the potential of lead leaching. Here, we highlight and discuss some of the common solutions for mitigating potential environmental and human health risks of PSMs, ranging from encapsulation strategies to alternative EoL handling options.

## _6.1. Encapsulation strategies_

## _6.1.1. External encapsulants_

External device encapsulation methods primarily focus on glass-glass vacuum lamination methods with a curable adhesive encapsulation to isolate the solar cells from the ambient environment. An effective

encapsulant must have an appropriate elastic modulus to hold the package tightly together [94]. Other important encapsulant characteristics are cost, compatibility with the low-temperature perovskite device fabrication processes, high dielectric breakdown to mitigate potentialinduced degradation, high resistivity, transparency ( _>_ 90 %), low water absorptivity, high light transmission, and excellent resistance to UV degradation and thermal oxidation [95,96]. Once encapsulated, the package is laminated through a vacuum step above 100[◦] C to prevent delamination caused by coefficient of thermal expansion mismatches between the perovskite active layer and/or mechanical stressors. To ensure adequate bonding and to avoid porosity during lamination, an appropriate volume of encapsulant must be selected to match the volume otherwise the edge seal will push out of place or void formation will occur [94]. To show the importance of encapsulation methodology, Jiang _et al._ performed a computational analysis describing how lead leakage rates significantly depend on the encapsulation methodology and reported that glass/adhesive/glass encapsulated modules leached lead 375 times less than unencapsulated modules [97]. A standard procedure to encapsulate and laminate PSMs effectively has not been developed but techniques used for other PV and LED technologies may provide a starting point for the best packaging architectures for PSMs [10,95,98–100].

## _6.1.2. Barrier films_

Barrier film strategies, such as grain boundary and interface encapsulation techniques may also be employed to impede or inhibit the active material (i.e. lead) from moving within the device itself [10]. Grain boundary encapsulation is the process of introducing additives to

the perovskite precursor to help prevent moisture and oxygen exposure to the perovskite grain boundaries [101,102]. Liu _et al._ showed that a nanoscale encapsulation method using silica oligomers at the grains of a FA-based perovskite protected the device from environmental stressors while enhancing the thermal stability [102]. For interfacial encapsulation, hydrophobic polymers with long side chains, among others, have been investigated to keep water out of the device [10]. Examples of long side chain polymers include, aminovaleric acid iodide, alkylalkoxysilane, hydrophobic thiols, oleic acid, and polydimethylsiloxane [10]. The long side chain polymers are typically implemented at the interface between the perovskite and carrier transport layer to prevent exposure to water and/or oxygen. Although many researchers use these techniques to prevent moisture and oxygen ingress at the grain boundaries and interfaces, the commercial opportunity for PSM encapsulants mainly lies with external encapsulation techniques due to scalability and TRL.

## _6.2. Sequestration layers_

Sequestration layers and materials can be implemented into the active layer or outer electrode surface used in PSMs to trap lead from leaching into the environment. Sequestration layer technologies include functionalized nanoparticles and other chemical approaches to sequester an active material (i.e. lead) to prevent leaching. Mendez _et al._ showed that thiol-functionalized nanospheres provide a low-cost solution to minimize lead leaching [103]. Li _et al_ . proposed a chemical approach that applies a transparent lead absorbing molecular film to the front side of a transparent conductive electrode that captured 96 % of the potential lead leakage. In a follow up study, Li _et al_ . presented a lead absorbing tape and layered both sides of the device to mimic a standard encapsulation processes used for Si-based solar cells [104]. To test the utility of this method, a device with the lead absorbing tape was first exposed to outdoor conditions for three months followed by severe damage, then smashed with a hammer, cut with a knife, and submerged in water to evaluate the tape’s effectiveness [105]. After a seven day submersion, the tape absorbed the lead, swelled up rather than dissolved, and captured 99.9 % of the potential lead leakage.

## _6.3. Metal organic frameworks (MOFs)_

Metal organic frameworks (MOFs) are crystalline organic and inorganic porous materials constructed by metal ions and organic ligands through coordination bonds and can be constructed at various perovskite nanocrystal interfaces in a device to store the nanocrystals within the MOF pores [106]. The MOF pore size acts as a mesh to separate perovskite nanocrystals which is beneficial for stabilization and the prevention of lead leaching. Therefore, selecting appropriate MOFs with sufficient pore size for the perovskite is required for a desired performance that helps address two key barriers to commercializing PSCs: stability and environmental lead toxicity [107]. However, the MOFs for perovskite technology is still in its infancy and the scalability and manufacturability are still unproven [108]. As an example. Dong _et al._ constructed a novel chemical doping strategy to assemble a stable MOF system for PSCs [109]. This approach led to high performance and longterm air stability by retaining 85 % of its initial PCE over 1000 h in ambient conditions while restricting lead leaching from the degraded PSC.

## _6.4. End of life management strategies_

The TCLP is currently the predominant EPA recognized method used to characterize PV modules as hazardous or non-hazardous waste. As an alternative approach for a hazardous waste determination, Section 1.2 of Method 1311 allows for a total analysis. However, TCLP testing or “generator knowledge” may still need to be used, if the total analysis does not demonstrate that the PSM contains no regulated materials or

the regulated materials are at such low concentrations that even if 100 % of the regulated material leached out the regulatory threshold would still not be met [110]. The use of “generator knowledge” is also an allowable regulatory pathway for hazardous waste determination that is separate from Method 1311 [111]. Acceptable forms of generator knowledge may include process knowledge, knowledge of feedstocks for manufacturing, knowledge of by-products and/or intermediates produced during manufacturing, and knowledge of chemical or physical properties. Further investigation is ongoing to explore the regulatory pathway of using generator knowledge to make hazardous waste determinations for PV modules [111,112].

Regulations and available services to recycle PSMs are strategies to avoid storage of PSMs or disposal in landfills where potential leaching may occur. Manufacturer take-back and recycling services are in place in the EU and other mature PV markets where PV module recycling is required. Regulations are emerging in the U.S. at the state level regarding recycling of PV technologies and a small number of individual manufacturers even offer take-back and recycling services (First Solar, SunPower/Maxeon, and REC Group) [69]. Starting July 1, 2025, Washington State will be the first state to require PV module manufacturers to offer and finance PV module take-back for reuse or recycling of products to be sold within or into the state.

Research into the recyclability of PSMs suggests that the solubility of lead halides may aid in recovering lead and other materials at low cost and high purity, enabling use of recovered materials in new PSMs [74,113]. Kim _et al_ . summarizes two recycling approaches: 1) selective lead extraction, in which the perovskite layer dissolves into solution for lead recovery to be reused in new PSM fabrications; and 2) in-situ processing, in which the perovskite layer is regenerated [79]. One challenge with selective layer by layer separations is the utilization of different solvents that may result in lead impurities which are difficult to remove [77,79]. Two solvents that have been previously used to dissolve leadbased perovskites or by-products are deep eutectic solvents and molten salts [114,115]. Potential benefits of using a molten salt over chemical solvents are the avoidance of harmful chemicals altogether, high recovery rates, and low costs. One in-situ approach to aid in the recycling of PSMs is the immersion of degraded PSCs in a methylammonium iodide (CH3NH3I) solution for a period of months or chlorobenzene followed by thermal deposition to restore the PCE [116,117]. While in-situ approaches are an active area of study with the potential for low cost, Kim _et al_ . contends that challenges remain to successfully convert the PbI2 layer to a new perovskite layer through sequential deposition before in-situ strategies can be fully realized [79].

Recycling approaches specific to perovskite/silicon tandem module designs are emerging, using treatments such as thermal delamination and chemical cleaning [76]. One identified challenge for refabricating tandem devices is the nuance of not affecting the silicon or perovskite device while recycling or refurbishing the other. One example of refurbishing a perovskite/silicon tandem module was performed by Yang _et al_ . who demonstrated the complete removal of PbI2 using a dimethyl sulfoxide solvent while maintaining a comparable silicon solar cell efficiency to the original device. Overall, the remanufactured tandem device displayed minimal drops in performance after two rounds of recycling and refabrication [76].

For all candidate recycling treatments under development, further investigation, optimization, and scale up will be necessary to evaluate the cost, feasibility of fabricating new PSMs with recovered material, and environmental impacts. While the discussion here is focused on the recycling, reusing, and/or refurbishing of perovskite devices, proper management and cost-effective strategies for recycling, reusing, and/or refurbishing the other assembly components, such as epoxy resins, polyolefins, PIB, will also need further consideration [78].

## **7. Conclusion**

PSMs are an emerging PV technology that can be manufactured cost

effectively while maintaining PCE parity with current PV technologies in the market. However, the most efficient PSMs, to date, contain lead halides which may potentially pose environmental and human health risks as lead halides are more soluble in water than lead ions found in other PV technologies. The potential exposure pathways for PSMs that pose potential risks to environmental and human health include inhalation, skin contact, ingestion, and leaching into soil or groundwater with the potential exposure opportunities spanning from manufacturing to EoL management. While there are no commercial PSMs available today, understanding and creating solutions to mitigate potential environmental and human health risks would be beneficial in helping commercialize the technology.

U.S. regulations and standards exist by several U.S. regulatory agencies and standard organizations such as the EPA, USFWS, OSHA, local and state governments, IEC, ASTM, and ISO that would apply to PSMs, though not specific to PSMs, to reduce potential environmental and human health risks. Most of the U.S. regulations pertain to potential lead exposure and contamination, while standards published by IEC and ISO, aim to standardize PV product and manufacturing quality. PSMs are not the first emergent PV technology. CdTe, CIGS, and other thin-film modules have moved beyond their emergent technology status and are now commercial technologies despite containing hazardous materials, like cadmium and selenium. Strategies that were implemented for these successfully commercialized PV module technologies offer pathways for PSMs to overcome potential environmental and human health risks. For example, recycling services, module takeback programs, and robust packaging through engineered designs are approaches that PSM manufacturers can leverage. While inspiration can be taken from the existing solutions and technologies, modification or adaptation will likely be required to better suit the unique business development and innovation opportunities of the PSM industry.

Several areas of testing and experimentation that could be performed to help further understand the potential environmental and human health risks pertaining to PSMs are fire testing, in-field leach testing on aged and damaged modules, and investigation into alternative TCLP sampling methods. Fire testing would provide insight into the potential risk of toxic smoke generation which has implications for first responders and nearby populations. The impacts to groundwater and soil quality from extinguishing or stormwater runoff after the fire has been extinguished could also be assessed to determine the potential risks. An in-field damage simulation study would be valuable to determine the susceptibility of PSMs to lead leaching as a function of rainfall, exposure to environmental stressors, or other modes of damage. Further investigation into processes and procedures for TCLP testing to classify EoL PSMs as hazardous or non-hazardous is needed as current sampling methods utilize waterjet cutting that may result in inaccurate TCLP results and potentially contaminate the waterjet fluid. Lastly, studying what damage arises as a function of service life and what damage causes the highest likelihood of lead leaching would be important in providing insight into assembly design solutions to mitigate potential environmental and human health risks.

To mitigate and minimize potential environmental and human health risks several strategies and technologies are being pursued, such as external and internal encapsulants, sequestration layers, and MOFs. While these strategies are promising and reduce opportunities for potential lead leaching, it is unknown how each technology may affect the PSM commercialization potential. PSMs are an emerging PV technology that have potential to perform similarly to current PV modules with lower manufacturing costs, and as PSMs continue toward commercialization, several potential environmental and human health risks should be further investigated to understand how to potentially de-risk if deployed.
